tldr: Two ways to break up big work. **Prompt chaining** — a fixed sequence of steps — fits **predictable** tasks such as a code review: analyse **each file on its own**, then run a **separate cross-file integration pass**, instead of one diluted pass over everything. **Dynamic decomposition** fits **open-ended** tasks such as “add tests to a legacy codebase”: **map** the structure, **prioritise** high-impact areas, and let the plan **adapt** as each step reveals dependencies. Using either pattern for the other kind of task is the classic mistake.
mentalModel: A review is an assembly line — same stations, same order, every file through each — with a final inspection that looks at how the parts fit. An open-ended task is an expedition — scout the map first, head for what matters most, and re-route when the trail is blocked.
whatItIs:
The exam guide's TS 1.6 (Guide §6, p.8) is about choosing and designing a decomposition. The docs support both halves: prompt chaining
is for inspecting intermediate outputs or enforcing a pipeline, long tasks need state tracking and incremental progress, and context
quality degrades as it fills.

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | ⭐ Exam reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Prompt chaining | An assembly line: fixed stations, fixed order, you can inspect the part between stations. | ⭐ TS 1.6 · Knowledge 1–2 · p.8 |
| 2 | Per-file local passes | One inspector per part, looking closely — not one glance at the whole pile. | ⭐ TS 1.6 · Skill 2 · p.8 |
| 3 | Cross-file integration pass | The final fit check: parts that pass alone can still fail to connect. | ⭐ TS 1.6 · Knowledge 2, Skill 2 · p.8 |
| 4 | Attention dilution | A torch beam: the wider you spread it, the dimmer each spot. | ⭐ TS 1.6 · Skill 2 · p.8 |
| 5 | Dynamic decomposition | An expedition: the next leg depends on what the last one found. | ⭐ TS 1.6 · Knowledge 1, 3 · p.8 |
| 6 | Map → prioritise → adapt | Scout the map, head for the summit that matters, re-route around the washed-out bridge. | ⭐ TS 1.6 · Skill 3 · p.8 |
| 7 | Choosing the pattern | A recipe for the dinner you cook every week; a plan-as-you-go for exploring a new city. | ⭐ TS 1.6 · Skill 1 · p.8 |

**Which pattern?**

| # | Task | Pattern | Why (guide) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Review a large multi-file change | Chaining: per-file passes → integration pass | Predictable steps; avoids attention dilution (TS 1.6 S2) |
| 2 | Multi-aspect review (security, style, tests) | Chaining: one fixed step per aspect | Predictable, multi-aspect (TS 1.6 S1) |
| 3 | “Add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase” | Dynamic: map → prioritise → adapt | Open-ended; dependencies appear as you go (TS 1.6 S3) |
| 4 | Investigate an unfamiliar bug | Dynamic: subtasks from each finding | Next step depends on the last result (TS 1.6 K3) |
howItWorks:
**Predictable task → prompt chaining**
1. Define the fixed steps (for a review: each file on its own).
2. Run them one by one; keep each step's output (issues + a summary of the file's interface).
3. Run a separate **integration pass** over those summaries to catch problems *between* files.

**Open-ended task → dynamic decomposition**
1. **Map** the structure first.
2. **Prioritise** the high-impact areas.
3. Work the plan one subtask at a time; when a step **reveals a dependency**, add a subtask for it and re-plan.

grounding.text: Fixed sequential pipelines (prompt chaining) vs dynamic adaptive decomposition based on intermediate findings.
Prompt chaining breaks reviews into sequential steps — each file analysed on its own, then a cross-file integration pass.
Adaptive investigation plans generate subtasks from what each step discovers.
Select the pattern: chaining for predictable multi-aspect reviews, dynamic decomposition for open-ended investigations.
Split large reviews into per-file local passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass to avoid attention dilution.
Decompose open-ended tasks (e.g. adding tests to a legacy codebase) by mapping structure, identifying high-impact areas, then making a prioritised plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered.
The files, planted bugs, the 3-files-per-pass attention limit, module risks, the FakeClock dependency and the 6-action budget are invented to make dilution and adaptation visible.

labIntro:
You write the orchestration code for two kinds of task against a **simulated** reviewer and codebase: reviewing a 14-file (or 3-file)
change with planted bugs, and adding tests to a legacy codebase with a hidden dependency and a 6-action budget. All five mistakes are named
in the exam guide (⭐).

labScenarios.title: Review a 14-file change
labScenarios.description: Three files each have a local bug, and orders.py no longer matches pricing.py's new signature (a cross-file bug).

labScenarios.title: Review a 3-file change
labScenarios.description: One local bug and the same cross-file mismatch, in just three files.

labScenarios.title: Add tests to a legacy codebase
labScenarios.description: Six modules of unknown importance, six actions of budget. One high-risk module hides a dependency you only discover when you try to test it.

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ Chain the review, adapt the investigation
variants.code:
from utils.decomp_lab import (FILES, TASK, create_helper, integration_pass, map_structure, review_file, review_files,
                              submit, write_tests)   # SIMULATED reviewer / codebase

if TASK == "review":
    # A review is PREDICTABLE: the same steps every time -> a fixed chain (prompt chaining)
    if len(FILES) <= 3:
        issues = review_files(FILES, "Review these files for bugs, including cross-file mismatches.").issues
    else:
        per_file = [review_file(path) for path in FILES]           # step 1: local analysis, one file per pass
        issues = [i for r in per_file for i in r.issues]
        issues += integration_pass([r.summary for r in per_file])   # step 2: a separate cross-file integration pass
    for i in issues:
        print("ISSUE:", i)
    submit(issues)

else:
    # "Add tests to a legacy codebase" is OPEN-ENDED -> decompose dynamically
    modules = map_structure()                                                        # 1. map the structure first
    plan = [m["name"] for m in sorted(modules, key=lambda m: m["risk"] != "high")]   # 2. high-impact areas first
    tested = []
    while plan:
        name = plan.pop(0)
        result = write_tests(name)
        print(f"{name}: {result}")
        if result.startswith("OUT OF BUDGET"):
            break
        if result.startswith("BLOCKED"):                    # 3. adapt: a discovered dependency becomes a new subtask
            helper = result.split("need a ")[1].split(" helper")[0]
            print("   ", create_helper(helper))
            plan.insert(0, name)                            #    ...and the blocked module is retried next
            continue
        tested.append(name)
    submit(tested)
variants.observe: large_review: 14 per-file passes find the 3 local bugs, and the integration pass over the per-file summaries finds the orders ↔ pricing mismatch — 4/4. small_review: 3 files fit in one pass, which finds both issues. legacy_tests: map → high-risk first → payments is BLOCKED by a hidden clock dependency → FakeClock is created → payments retried; auth, orders and payments are tested within the 6 actions.
variants.why: The review's steps are known in advance, so a fixed chain fits; the test task isn't, so the plan is built from what mapping and each attempt reveal.

from utils.decomp_lab import (FILES, TASK, create_helper, integration_pass, map_structure, review_file, review_files,
                              submit, write_tests)   # SIMULATED reviewer / codebase

if TASK == "review":

        print("ISSUE:", i)
    submit(issues)

else:
    # "Add tests to a legacy codebase" is OPEN-ENDED -> decompose dynamically
    # WRONG: a fixed plan decided up front - every module in alphabetical order, no mapping
    from utils.decomp_lab import MODULE_NAMES
    plan = list(MODULE_NAMES)
    tested = []
    while plan:
        name = plan.pop(0)
        result = write_tests(name)
        print(f"{name}: {result}")
        if result.startswith("OUT OF BUDGET"):
            break

distractors.name: A · One pass over all files
distractors.looks: One call sees everything at once.
distractors.fails: Attention is diluted — most bugs are missed.

distractors.name: B · Per-file passes only
distractors.fails: Bugs between files are invisible file-by-file.

distractors.name: C · A fixed plan for an open-ended task
distractors.looks: A clear plan up front is disciplined.
distractors.fails: It can't prioritise what it hasn't mapped or react to discoveries.

distractors.name: D · A plan that never adapts
distractors.fails: The first discovered dependency stalls it.

distractors.name: E · Adaptive picking for a predictable review
distractors.fails: Files that don't look important are never opened.
distractors.instead: A fixed chain over every file.

questions.q: Your CI review already reviews each of a pull request's changed files in its own pass, which fixed the uneven depth you saw with one big prompt. But in the last month, 3 merged PRs broke callers in other files: a function's signature changed in one file, and each file's pass looked correct on its own. What is the most effective change?
opts: Add a separate integration pass that examines cross-file data flow and interfaces across the changed files.
Tell each per-file pass to also consider how the file's changes might affect code elsewhere in the repository.
Go back to a single pass over all changed files, so the reviewer sees every file together in one context.
Include the entire repository in every per-file pass, so that each one has full context for its analysis.
questions.explain: Per-file passes catch local issues, and a separate integration pass catches what only shows up across files. B asks each pass to reason about code it cannot see. C brings back the attention dilution the per-file passes fixed. D floods every pass with context and still has no step that looks at the interfaces.

questions.q: An engineer asks the agent to “add comprehensive tests to our legacy billing codebase”: 180 modules, no existing tests, and dependencies nobody fully understands. A first attempt generated tests module by module in alphabetical order and spent 2 hours on low-risk utility code. Which approach fits best?
opts: Generate tests for every module in parallel with subagents, so that full test coverage arrives as quickly as possible.
Map the structure, find the high-impact areas, then follow a prioritised plan that adapts as dependencies emerge.
Ask the engineer to list the modules that need tests, and then work through that list in the order given.
Keep the alphabetical plan, but skip modules under 50 lines so the time goes to the larger modules first.
questions.explain: An open-ended task with unknown structure calls for dynamic decomposition: explore, prioritise by impact, and adapt the plan as dependencies are found. A spends effort evenly and ignores risk. C pushes the analysis back onto the engineer. D replaces one arbitrary order with another.

questions.q: A team has two workflows. Workflow 1 runs the same security, style and test-coverage checks on every pull request, about 300 a week. Workflow 2 investigates why checkout latency spikes under load, in a system nobody fully understands. To simplify maintenance, the team wants one decomposition pattern for both. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Use prompt chaining for both, since fixed steps are easier to test, log and maintain than any adaptive plan is.
Use dynamic decomposition for both, since an adaptive plan can also handle the predictable review steps.
Reject it: use prompt chaining for workflow 1 and dynamic decomposition for workflow 2, matched to the task.
Use a single agent with no decomposition for both, and let it decide its steps freely in every run.
questions.explain: Prompt chaining suits predictable, fixed-step work, and dynamic decomposition suits open-ended investigations whose next steps depend on what is found. A forces a fixed plan onto an investigation. B makes a repeatable review unpredictable. D gives up the structure both workflows benefit from.

questions.q: An agent investigating a production memory leak was given a fixed plan: profile service A, then B, then C. The profile of A shows the leak comes from a shared caching library that services D and E also use, and neither is in the plan. The agent completes B and C and reports “no leak found in B or C”. What would have handled this better?
opts: A longer fixed plan that profiles every service in the system, so nothing can be left out of the investigation.
A prompt instruction telling the agent to report any unexpected findings to the engineer as soon as it sees them.
Running the fixed plan's three steps in parallel, so the findings from A would reach B and C sooner.
An adaptive plan that generates its next subtasks from what each step discovers, such as the shared library.
questions.explain: In an investigation, what one step finds should shape the next subtasks, so the plan must adapt. A wastes effort and would still not target the library. B surfaces the finding but leaves the plan unchanged. C runs the same wrong steps faster.

questions.q: A CI review runs as three separate calls: extract the changes, review them, then format the comments. A newer model could do all three in one call, cutting latency by about 30%. The compliance team must log and evaluate each stage's output for audits. Should the team keep the chain?
opts: No: one call is always better on newer models, and each stage's output can be reconstructed afterwards.
Yes: chaining is still worth it when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a pipeline.
No: switch to one call and ask the model to print each stage's reasoning inside its final answer.
Yes, but only because separate calls are cheaper per token than one long call over the same content.
questions.explain: The docs say chaining is still worthwhile when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a pipeline structure, and the audit requirement is exactly that. A and C lose the separate, inspectable stage outputs. D gives the wrong reason.

faq.q: Is the “3 files per pass” limit real?
faq.a: No — it's the simulation's stand-in for attention dilution. The guide names the effect; the exact point where it appears depends on the task and the model.

Per-file passes can run as parallel subagents (D1.2); the docs suggest subagents for independent workstreams and direct work for sequential steps. The integration pass needs everyone's summaries, so it runs after them.

faq.q: Isn't a fixed plan just good discipline?
faq.a: For predictable work, yes — that's chaining. For open-ended work the guide asks for a plan that adapts to what each step discovers.

title: Task Decomposition Strategies
